turns.prompt_text: I have some coaxial cables from antenna I've taken from different router systems and such The wires look fairly complicated for me to be able to connect to anything or resolder They might be useless but I'm not sure yet I know the connectors are these tiny little brass pieces or copper or whatever they are Attached 1 file. - 1661bdfb-3092-403c-a299-77fd9515b2fa
turns.response_html:
Based on the image in the file "1661bdfb-3092-403c-a299-77fd9515b2fa", these are standard omnidirectional dipole antennas, typically used for Wi-Fi routers, access points, or Bluetooth modules.

Your instincts are spot on—these are indeed coaxial cables, specifically micro-coaxial cables, and they are notoriously difficult to work with once cut.

Here is a breakdown of what you are looking at and whether they are worth keeping.

The Anatomy of the Wire

Even though the wire looks like a single strand, it is actually a complex, layered structure designed to carry high-frequency radio signals (like 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz) without interference. If you look closely at the longest exposed wire in the photo, you can see these layers:

  1. Inner Conductor: A microscopic wire in the very dead center that carries the actual signal.
  2. Dielectric Insulator: A tiny white plastic tube surrounding the center wire.
  3. Outer Shield (The Braid): The frayed metallic mesh you can see exposed on the longest wire. This acts as the ground and shields the inner signal from outside interference.
  4. Outer Jacket: The black or grey plastic coating on the outside.

The "Tiny Brass Pieces"

The connectors you mentioned are likely U.FL (or IPEX/MHF) connectors. They are tiny, snap-on brass or gold-plated terminals that press down onto mating nodes on a router's circuit board. Because of their microscopic size, crimping or soldering new U.FL connectors onto cut wires by hand is nearly impossible without highly specialized, expensive tooling.

Can You Resolder Them?

Technically, yes, but practically, it usually isn't worth the effort for RF (radio frequency) applications. Here is why:

  • Micro-Soldering Difficulty: You have to strip the wire, pull back the braided shield, strip the microscopic insulator, and solder the inner core to a board without the outer shield and inner core ever touching. If a single microscopic hair of the braided shield touches the inner conductor, the antenna shorts out and becomes useless.
  • Impedance Mismatch: Wi-Fi antennas and their cables are precisely tuned (usually to 50 ohms). When you cut, splice, or solder a micro-coaxial cable, you alter the physical geometry of the wire. This creates an "impedance mismatch." Instead of the Wi-Fi signal traveling smoothly out of the antenna, a large portion of the signal reflects back into the router, resulting in terrible range, dropped packets, or even a burnt-out radio chip.

The Verdict: Are They Useless?

For their original intended purpose as Wi-Fi or Bluetooth antennas, yes, these are practically useless in their current cut state.

Unless you are looking for a punishingly difficult micro-soldering challenge for practice, the labor and signal loss aren't worth it. Brand-new replacement antennas with intact micro-coaxial cables and pre-attached U.FL connectors can be bought online for just a few dollars.
